#10733. CodeAgents + Structure: A Better Way to Execute Actions

Today we're sharing research that bridges two powerful paradigms in AI agent design: the expressiveness of code-based actions and the reliability of structured generation. Our findings show that forcing CodeAgents to generate both thoughts and code in a structured JSON format can significantly outperform traditional approaches across multiple benchmarks.

Figure 1: Accuracy comparison of three approaches: Structured CodeAgent (blue), CodeAgent (orange), and ToolCallingAgent (gray) on SmolBench (GAIA, MATH, SimpleQA, and Frames). Error bars represent 95% Confidence Intervals.

AI agents need to take actions in the world - whether that's calling APIs, processing data, or reasoning through complex problems. How agents express these actions has evolved through several paradigms:

Traditional JSON Agent: Agents generate structured JSON to call tools.

These agents operate by selecting from a list of predefined tools and generating JSON-formatted calls. This method for calling tools has been popularized by OpenAI's function calling API, and has since then been the most widely used method to call tools.

Code Agents: Agents make use of their innate coding ability and write executable Python code directly.

This shift, first presented as CodeAct in the paper “Executable Code Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents” gave AI agents the flexibility to write arbitrary executable Python code in addition to tool-calling.

The key insight here is that tools are called directly from within the code, making variables and state management much more reliable. Agents can call tools within loops, functions, and conditional statements - essentially generating a dynamic graph of tool execution in each action!

However, parsing code from markdown can be error-prone which leads us to a proposition: why not use structured generation to generate code actions?

With Structured outputs, you can force the LLM to generate explicit thoughts and code as a JSON blob:

The key difference is that the generation is enforced: basically, now instead of just being prompted to output thoughts, then code, the usage of structured outputs forces it to respect the structure.

This approach adds the reliability of structured generation to the flexibility of code execution, thus getting the best of both worlds.

We compared these three paradigms across multiple benchmarks including GAIA, MATH, SimpleQA, and Frames. The results show a clear pattern: Code actions + structured generation consistently improves performance for capable models.

Across most capable models, the structured approach consistently outperformed the regular CodeAgent approach by 2-7 percentage points on average.

Our implementation of CodeAgent in smolagents extracts Python code from the LLM output, which can fail when:

Structured generation eliminates these issues with reliable JSON parsing.

To understand why structured generation matters, we analyzed 15,724 agent traces across our benchmarks. The results are striking:

Agent traces without parsing errors succeed 21.3% more often than those with parsing errors.

This isn't just about convenience - parsing errors create a cascade of failures that significantly impact overall agent performance. When an agent can't execute its first action due to malformed code, it often struggles to recover, leading to suboptimal problem-solving paths.

Figure 2: Parsing errors in the first step reduce success rates of the agent by 21.3% and increase average steps taken from 3.18 to 4.63.

The use of structured generation and explicit thoughts not just prompts, but forces agents to articulate their reasoning before acting. This leads to:

Our results also reveal a clear capability threshold: models need sufficient instruction-following ability and JSON coverage in their pre-training data to benefit from structured generation. This suggests that structured approaches work best with:

Here's what happens when a smaller model (e.g mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3) tries to generate structured code - the cognitive load becomes too much:

The model generates syntactically broken Python code: web_search(query="Eiffel Tower height")", - notice the malformed string with an extra quote and comma. This leads to an immediate SyntaxError and execution failure.

This illustrates the "structure tax": smaller models struggle to simultaneously handle JSON formatting, Python syntax, and the actual problem-solving logic. The cognitive overhead of structured generation can overwhelm models that would otherwise perform reasonably well with simpler markdown-based code generation.

It’s super simple! Just enable it with use_structured_outputs_internally:

The LLM will generate something like this:

Then the "code" part gets executed by the agent as usual : this is the standard CodeAgent, but now it has 100% parsing reliability!

This research suggests we're moving toward a more nuanced understanding of agent architectures. It's not just about "what can the agent do?" but "how should the agent think about what it's doing?"

Maybe making the reasoning process more explicit helps the model stay on track. Or maybe it's just easier to parse. Either way, it’s a win.

But this is just the beginning. There are so many questions left to explore:

For now, if you're using smolagents (or building your own CodeAgent system), consider giving structured output a try. Your parsing errors will thank you, and you might just see a nice increase in performance!

Did you try YAML block scalars or Python triple-quoted strings? These require less escaping, so they might mitigate the "structure tax".

AI agents the flexibility to write arbitrary executable Python code in addition to tool-calling. The key insight here is that tools are called directly from within the code, making variables and state management much more reliable. Agents can call tools within loops, functions, and conditional statements - essentially generating a dynamic graph of tool execution in each actionhttps://spacebar-clicker.org/

#10732. How to Create Effective Cold Email Sequences That Generate Replies: A Developer's Guide

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Connecting with prospects via cold email isn't always straightforward, particularly when recipients receive dozens of messages every day. Even a relevant email can get lost in a crowded inbox. That's why many B2B companies use cold email sequences to maintain consistent communication and manage follow-ups.

However, creating effective email sequences involves more than writing messages and choosing sending intervals. Developers building or integrating email automation systems must also consider API reliability, message scheduling, data validation, email authentication, security, and workflow monitoring.

A well-designed email sequence combines relevant communication with reliable technical infrastructure. This article explains how to structure cold email sequences and explores the development practices that make automated email workflows more dependable.

A cold email sequence is a planned series of emails sent to prospective customers who have not previously established a direct relationship with the sender. These messages are delivered over a defined period, with each email designed to introduce an offer, provide additional context, address a potential concern, or encourage a response.

For example, a software development company might contact a growing SaaS business to discuss opportunities to improve its application infrastructure. The first email could introduce the company's expertise, the second could explain a relevant technical challenge, and the third could share a useful observation about application performance.

Each message supports the same overall objective while contributing something different.

From a developer's perspective, a cold email sequence can also be understood as an event-driven workflow. Every contact has a sequence state, scheduled messages, and conditions that determine whether the next message should be delivered.

A basic sequence might follow this structure:

This model is useful for developers working on CRM integrations, email platforms, customer engagement systems, and automated business workflows.

The first step is to establish a clear plan before writing any messages. Determine who you want to contact, what problem your offer solves, and what action you want recipients to take.

Start by defining your ideal customer profile, identifying relevant decision-makers, and researching their business needs. Next, select one primary campaign objective, such as generating positive replies, booking qualified meetings, or exploring potential partnerships.

Decide how many emails you will send, what each message will communicate, and how much time will pass between follow-ups. Make sure every email adds value instead of repeating information from previous messages.

For example, a software consultancy targeting B2B SaaS companies might introduce an application performance challenge in the first email, share a practical recommendation in the second, provide a relevant engineering case study in the third, and close the sequence with a polite final follow-up.

Before launching the campaign, review the prospect list, verify contact information, check email authentication, and test the complete sequence.

Developers should also establish technical requirements before implementation:

Define how contact information will be stored and validated.

Determine which events trigger scheduled emails.

Implement conditions that prevent unnecessary follow-ups.

Establish secure API connections between applications.

Record delivery results, failures, and recipient responses.

These considerations help transform a basic email campaign into a maintainable automation workflow.

Every cold email sequence needs a specific objective. Without one, messages may contain several unrelated offers or ask recipients to take different actions.

A SaaS company might want to schedule product demonstrations, while a software consultancy may want to connect with businesses planning infrastructure improvements. A recruitment firm might aim to establish relationships with technical hiring managers.

Your objective should influence the message and call to action.

For developers building campaign dashboards, goals should also be represented through measurable application events.

This example demonstrates how a dashboard might calculate a positive reply rate from stored campaign events.

In production, developers should also handle zero denominators, duplicate events, inconsistent reporting periods, and differences between accepted, delivered, and failed messages.

Effective cold email sequences begin with the right audience. Even a well-written email is unlikely to generate meaningful replies if it reaches people who have no interest in the subject.

Start by defining your ideal customer profile. Consider industry, company size, location, business model, growth stage, and the challenges your product or service addresses.

For example, a development consultancy offering cloud migration assistance might contact CTOs, engineering managers, and technical founders. Although these professionals may benefit from similar services, their priorities can differ.

A CTO may focus on infrastructure reliability and operational costs, while an engineering manager may prioritize deployment workflows, maintainability, and team productivity.

Segment prospects according to meaningful differences rather than sending identical messages to everyone.

Audience segmentation can be implemented through database queries, CRM filters, or API-based contact management.

A simplified contact object might look like this:

Structured data makes segmentation more predictable and helps prevent inconsistent personalization.

Contact data should be collected and processed lawfully, with appropriate access controls and retention policies.

Personalization helps prospects understand why you are contacting them specifically. However, effective personalization involves more than inserting a first name, company name, or job title into a template.

Research relevant professional information that connects the recipient's business to your offer.

For example, a development consultancy contacting a SaaS company could mention a recently announced application launch and explain how scalable deployment practices may support future growth.

The observation should be accurate and connected to a genuine technical challenge.

A practical personalization process involves three steps:

Identify a relevant professional observation.

Explain why it may matter to the recipient.

Connect it naturally to the proposed solution.

Developers can support this process with reusable templates and structured variables.

This simple example demonstrates template personalization.

In production, developers should validate template variables, prevent accidental disclosure of customer data, and escape untrusted values when generating HTML.

The subject line gives recipients an initial indication of what an email contains. A clear, relevant subject line helps them recognize the message's purpose.

Keep subject lines concise and connected to the recipient's business needs. Avoid exaggerated promises, artificial urgency, and misleading claims.

The best subject line depends on the audience and purpose.

Developers building email systems should also consider subject-line encoding, Unicode handling, template validation, and protection against header injection.

For example, email libraries should be responsible for constructing message headers rather than applications manually concatenating untrusted header strings.

SitePoint's tutorial on sending email using Node.js provides additional guidance on email construction and delivery.

The first email introduces your business and gives the prospect a reason to consider your offer.

A useful structure includes a personalized opening, a clear value proposition, a brief explanation of relevant expertise, and one simple call to action.

For example, a development consultancy contacting a SaaS business might explain that it helps software teams improve deployment workflows and application reliability.

Avoid introducing every service you offer or listing multiple benefits in the same email.

From a technical perspective, the first message should also establish the recipient's sequence state.

This state information allows a background worker to determine when an email is eligible for delivery.

Before sending, the worker must recheck the latest recipient status. A scheduled job should never override a newly recorded opt-out.

Subject: A question about your development workflow

I noticed [relevant observation about the company's software development process] and thought there might be an opportunity to improve deployment reliability.

Our team works with growing software companies on application infrastructure, development workflows, and performance improvements.

Is improving your development infrastructure a priority for your team this quarter?

The personalized observation should be specific and accurate. A concise message is more useful than a generic introduction filled with broad claims.

An effective cold email sequence follows a logical progression. Each message builds on the initial contact by introducing new information, clarifying value, or offering another way to engage.

Email sequencing tools can help teams schedule messages and manage follow-ups consistently. For developers integrating these systems into existing applications, it is important to understand how scheduling, contact states, reply events, and automation rules interact.

A five-email sequence can provide a practical starting point:

These intervals are starting points rather than universal rules. Adjust them to suit the audience, recipient preferences, and campaign performance.

For developers, scheduling is one of the most important technical aspects of email automation.

Sending messages directly inside an HTTP request can create unnecessary delays and make failure handling difficult.

A more reliable architecture uses background jobs.

This approach separates campaign management from email delivery.

For example, a worker can process scheduled messages independently while the main application continues handling user requests.

SitePoint's guide to implementing a task queue in Node.js explains how background processing can support workloads such as email delivery.

Production implementations should include persistent scheduling, retry policies, rate limiting, and idempotency controls to reduce duplicate messages.

Follow-up emails give prospects another opportunity to respond when they overlook an initial message or need additional information.

Each follow-up should introduce a useful detail, clarify the offer, or address a relevant concern.

For example, a software consultancy could use its first follow-up to explain a common deployment bottleneck. A later message might share a relevant case study or describe how the consultancy approaches application monitoring.

Subject: Re: A question about your development workflow

I wanted to follow up on my previous message.

One area worth reviewing is whether your deployment process includes automated testing, rollback procedures, and application performance monitoring.

These practices can help development teams identify problems earlier and improve release reliability.

Would a brief conversation about your current development workflow be useful?

This follow-up adds context without repeating the original message.

Stop the sequence when someone replies, opts out, or otherwise indicates that further contact is unwelcome.

Prospects receiving unsolicited emails may have little reason to trust an unfamiliar sender.

Relevant evidence helps establish credibility.

Social proof can include verified customer results, technical case studies, industry experience, or examples of previous work.

For example, a software consultancy might share a documented case study showing how automated testing reduced deployment failures.

When case studies are unavailable, demonstrate expertise through a practical observation or useful recommendation.

Developers building campaign systems should ensure that reusable case studies and message templates are versioned appropriately. This makes it easier to identify which content was sent and prevents outdated claims from being reused unintentionally.

Avoid exaggerated claims, invented statistics, and guarantees that cannot be supported.

A call to action tells the recipient what to do next.

In cold email outreach, a complicated request can discourage engagement because the prospect has not yet developed enough interest to commit time or resources.

Is this a priority for your team right now?

Would a short technical overview be useful?

Are you the right person to discuss this with?

Would you be open to exploring a potential partnership?

Choose a CTA that matches the purpose of the email.

Developers designing email templates should also consider accessibility. Links should use descriptive text, buttons should have sufficient contrast, and HTML emails should include readable plain-text alternatives.

Beyond content and scheduling, developers need to ensure that automated email workflows operate securely and consistently.

Email authentication helps receiving systems evaluate whether a message is authorized to use its sending domain.

SPF (Sender Policy Framework): Identifies servers authorized to send mail for a domain.

DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail): Uses cryptographic signatures to help verify message integrity and signing-domain responsibility.

DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance): Defines how SPF or DKIM authentication should align with the visible From domain and provides reporting capabilities.

Developers responsible for email infrastructure should understand how these mechanisms work together.

SitePoint's article on email deliverability provides additional context about authentication, sender reputation, and delivery reliability.

Modern email workflows often integrate CRM systems, databases, automation platforms, and email service providers.

REST APIs allow developers to exchange information between these applications.

For example, an application might synchronize contact records, create campaigns, retrieve reply events, or update sequence states.

When building integrations, developers should:

Avoid exposing sensitive information in logs.

These practices improve maintainability and reduce the risk of inconsistent campaign data.

Webhooks allow external platforms to notify applications when events occur.

A simplified event handler could look like this:

This example illustrates application-level event handling rather than a particular provider's webhook format.

A production webhook endpoint must verify the provider's authentication or signature mechanism before processing events. It should also handle duplicate deliveries, out-of-order events, and temporary database failures.

Testing is essential when an application sends automated messages.

Messages are scheduled at the correct times.

Failed jobs do not create duplicate messages.

Templates render correctly across email clients.

API failures produce useful operational logs.

Tools such as Postman, Mailpit, and automated integration tests can help validate different parts of the workflow.

Use synthetic recipients and controlled test environments rather than sending test campaigns to real prospects.

Developers building campaign dashboards or CRM-connected applications may need to integrate an external sequencing platform rather than implement every sending feature themselves.

EmailBison is one example of a platform for managing cold email campaigns and follow-ups. Its API and integration capabilities make it relevant when evaluating how a third-party email system can fit into an existing application architecture.

For developers, the main consideration is not simply whether a platform can schedule messages, but how its capabilities interact with the application's data model and operational requirements.

For example, a CRM integration might follow this workflow:

This architecture introduces several engineering considerations.

Data synchronization: Contact records must remain consistent between the CRM and the email platform.

Error handling: API failures should be recorded and retried safely when appropriate.

Security: API credentials and contact information should be protected.

Observability: Developers should be able to investigate failed operations without exposing sensitive information.

The same architectural principles apply to other email automation providers. Before choosing an integration, review its current API documentation, authentication model, event coverage, rate limits, and data-handling requirements.

Several common mistakes can reduce the effectiveness and reliability of cold email outreach, even when businesses use automation.

Sending generic messages: Emails that could apply to any business fail to establish relevance. Use appropriate segmentation and accurate personalization.

Repeating the same pitch: Every follow-up should contribute something new instead of repeating the original message.

Making emails too long: Excessive explanations and multiple offers make it harder for prospects to identify the main point.

Using aggressive follow-ups: Sending messages too frequently can frustrate recipients. Choose reasonable intervals and respect recipient preferences.

Making unsupported claims: Exaggerated results and misleading promises damage credibility.

Ignoring recipient responses: Stop automated sequences when someone replies, opts out, or requests no further contact.

Failing to handle duplicate events: A webhook may be delivered more than once. Applications should use idempotent processing to avoid repeated actions.

Ignoring API failures: Temporary provider outages and rate limits should not silently corrupt campaign state.

Insufficient testing: Automation workflows should be validated with controlled test data before production deployment.

Scaling too quickly: Increasing sending volume before validating deliverability, infrastructure, and workflow reliability can amplify existing problems.

Avoiding these mistakes helps teams maintain a professional communication process while reducing operational risks.

A cold email sequence can start with three to five emails, including the initial message and follow-ups. The appropriate number depends on the audience, purpose, and recipient preferences.

Focus on providing useful information rather than increasing the number of messages unnecessarily.

Yes. Developers can integrate email sequencing platforms with web applications through APIs, webhooks, and background workers.

Common use cases include CRM synchronization, campaign dashboards, reply tracking, and workflow automation.

A practical starting point is two to four days before the first follow-up, followed by slightly longer intervals between later messages.

The schedule should account for recipient preferences and stop immediately when further contact is unwanted.

Yes. Sequencing tools can automate scheduling, follow-ups, contact management, and reply detection.

Human oversight remains important for message quality, data accuracy, security, and responding appropriately to interested prospects.

Testing should also verify that automated messages are not sent to suppressed contacts.

Yes. Small businesses may prioritize straightforward communication and immediate practical benefits, while enterprise prospects may require more information about security, integration, scalability, and stakeholder approval.

From a development perspective, enterprise integrations may also require stronger access controls, audit logging, and data synchronization.

Creating effective cold email sequences requires relevant messaging, thoughtful follow-ups, and reliable automation.

For developers, the underlying technical systems are just as important as the messages themselves. Contact validation, background scheduling, API integrations, email authentication, webhook processing, and error handling all contribute to dependable email workflows.

By treating email sequencing as a structured, event-driven application process rather than simply a series of scheduled messages, development teams can build systems that are easier to test, monitor, maintain, and extend.

The goal is not merely to send more emails. It is to create a reliable communication workflow that respects recipients and supports meaningful conversations.

#10731. No GPU left behind: Unlocking Efficiency with Co-located vLLM in TRL

TRL supports training LLMs using GRPO, an online learning algorithm recently introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper. In GRPO, the model learns from its own outputs: it generates responses during training, receives feedback, and uses that feedback to improve itself over time.

This makes generation a critical step in the training loop — and also a major bottleneck. To speed up generation, TRL integrates with vLLM. This combination lets you train powerful models more efficiently in GRPO setup. However, there’s a catch.

Before TRL v0.18.0, vLLM was only supported in server mode, running as a separate process on different GPUs from the training job. It communicated with the training script over HTTP, which made the setup modular and easy to use — but also introduced GPU inefficiencies.

This “ping-pong” between training and generation causes:

In online learning methods like GRPO — where generation happens constantly — this inefficiency becomes even more painful. You spend more on hardware, but don't get the performance you'd expect.

So, the key question becomes: Can we share the same GPUs for both training and generation, instead of separating them?

The main issue was that training and inference ran on separate GPUs, leading to idle time and underutilization. The natural solution? Run both on the same GPUs. Instead of having vLLM operate as a standalone server in its own process and devices, what if vLLM could run alongside the training code, within the same distributed process group? This would let us launch a single distributed job where training and inference share the same devices, switching between tasks efficiently without wasting resources.

This approach is what we refer to as colocation. Training and inference are co-located on the same GPUs and coordinated via the same process group, allowing them to take turns smoothly — no extra hardware needed.

Previously, this wasn’t possible in TRL, which relied on vLLM as an external HTTP server. That changed with our PR #3394, which added support for vLLM’s external launcher and true integration into the training process.

Unified Execution: By embedding vLLM in the same process group, both training and inference tasks can share the same GPUs, taking turns instead of waiting on each other. This reduces idle time and boosts overall efficiency.

Skip HTTP Communication: No need for REST API calls or networking — vLLM runs inline with the training loop, avoiding overhead and latency.

Torchrun Compatibility: Works seamlessly with torchrun, so it's easy to scale across nodes with minimal config changes.

TP and DP Support: Compatible with Tensor Parallelism and Data Parallelism, making it suitable for large-scale training runs.

SPMD Execution Pattern: Uses a Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) model, where each GPU runs its own instance of the engine in sync. Ideal for distributed multi-GPU, multi-node setups.

Simplified Deployment: You no longer need to maintain a separate server script — vLLM is launched and controlled directly inside your training job.

Enhanced Throughput: By avoiding idle GPUs and eliminating inter-process communication, the system delivers faster training and generation, especially important in online learning setups like GRPO.

Robust Inter-process Communication: This is more robust because it avoids the complexity of setting up distributed process groups between independent processes, as required in server mode.

Thanks to this feature, co-located training and inference is no longer a hack — it’s now first-class, scalable, and production-ready.

The shift from server TRL to co-located TRL is all about smarter GPU usage. The diagram below shows the difference:

In the server TRL setup, training and inference run on separate GPUs. For example:

During training steps, GPU 3 sits idle. During generation steps (inference), GPUs 0–2 are idle while GPU 3 generates outputs.

In contrast, the co-located TRL setup runs both training and vLLM on the same GPUs. Each GPU:

Training and inference take turns using the GPU’s resources — no need for dedicated devices or separate processes.

Instead of launching vLLM as a server, the trainer now launches vLLM in-process using the external launcher, as shown below:

Co-located vLLM respects the torch.distributed process group and rank structure. This allows vLLM to be initialized alongside training without conflict and makes TP/DP setups work seamlessly:

Co-located vLLM no longer relies on REST APIs — it runs directly in memory and communicates via native Python calls:

To use this setup, simply set vllm_mode="colocate" in your GRPO configuration:

Note: Depending on the model size and the overall GPU memory requirements for training, you may need to adjust the vllm_gpu_memory_utilization parameter in GRPOConfig to avoid underutilization or out-of-memory errors.

To measure the impact of colocation, we ran a series of experiments comparing the traditional server mode (where vLLM runs on a separate GPU as a standalone server) with the new co-locate mode (where training and inference share the same GPUs).

In server mode, only 7 GPUs are used for training because 1 GPU is fully dedicated to the vLLM inference server.

In co-locate mode, all 8 GPUs are used for training — increasing the effective batch size by default.

To ensure a fair comparison, we normalized throughput in server mode by a factor of 8/7. This adjustment accounts for the greater training capacity in co-locate mode and allows us to compare the two setups under equal training conditions.

When training large models like Qwen2.5-Math-72B, it's important to use the right strategies to make training efficient, scalable, and stable across many GPUs and nodes. In our setup, we combined co-located vLLM with several key optimizations to make this work efficiently.

When using co-located training, managing GPU memory is crucial so that both training and inference can run smoothly on the same devices. To support this, we added vLLM’s sleep() API into the GRPO training loop.

The sleep() function temporarily pauses the vLLM engine and frees up GPU memory. It supports two levels:

Level 1: Unloads model weights from GPU (keeps them in CPU memory) and clears the KV cache. Useful when the same model will be reused soon.

Level 2: Unloads both model weights and KV cache entirely. Best for scenarios where the model will change or won’t be reused right away.

In GRPO, the model is updated after every step — so we use Level 2 sleep.

This small addition makes a big difference in enabling smooth and scalable co-located training.

To train large models like Qwen2.5-72B, we rely on DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3, the same setup used in plain TRL.

ZeRO helps scale large models by distributing memory across GPUs. Stage 3 goes further by partitioning:

This is essential for models that can’t fit on a single GPU. With ZeRO Stage 3, each GPU handles only a portion of the model.

"offload_optimizer": {"device": "cpu"} Moves optimizer states to CPU to free GPU memory — critical in co-located setups.

"overlap_comm": true Enables communication overlap with computation, speeding up training.

"contiguous_gradients": true Allocates gradients in a single memory block, improving memory access and reducing fragmentation.

These optimizations help train 72B models efficiently, and ensure colocation remains stable under tight memory constraints.

As recommended in TRL, we use Accelerate, a lightweight library that simplifies distributed training. It handles:

This makes the setup clean, scalable, and easy to maintain.

Even with 4 fewer GPUs, the co-locate setup is ~1.26× faster than plain TRL. This highlights the effectiveness of smarter GPU sharing and memory cleanup using sleep().

Training reward plots for co-locate and plain setups are nearly identical, demonstrating that:

We evaluated three models: Base model, Co-locate-trained model, Plain-trained model on the Math500 benchmark. Both trained models outperform the base, and the co-locate model performs on par with the plain-trained model — confirming that colocation does not compromise downstream performance.

Through our work on scaling GRPO training with co-located vLLM, we've faced several critical challenges and learned important lessons about efficiency, flexibility, and system design when training large models.

Tensor Parallelism Bug in vLLM ≥ 0.8.0. Tensor Parallelism (TP) with external_launcher stopped working in vLLM version 0.8.0 and above. This was tracked under Issue #15895. To identify the breaking point, we followed the approach described in this vLLM developer blog post, which provides wheels for every commit. After bisecting, we identified the breaking commit as cc10281. The root cause was determinism — the newer versions required explicitly setting the random seed. Once the seed was set, the issue went away.

Level 2 Sleep Buffer Bug. Initially, level 2 sleep didn’t work correctly when we tried to reload weights using load_weights. This issue was tracked in Issue #16564. The problem was that model buffers (like running mean/var in BatchNorm) weren’t restored after waking up from sleep. The fix came with PR #16889, which added logic to explicitly restore buffers when waking up from level 2 sleep. We now keep a copy of the original buffers and manually reapply them after loading new weights.

Segmentation Fault on Exit. There’s still an open issue with vLLM sleep causing a segmentation fault at the end of training when closing processes. This was reported in Issue #16993. This crash happens during shutdown but does not break training itself, so we were able to complete all demos and experiments shared in this blog. However, we’re waiting for an official fix before integrating sleep() fully into TRL upstream.

These challenges were not blockers, but they required careful debugging, version control, and a deeper understanding of how vLLM manages memory and parallelism under the hood.

Co-located inference dramatically improves GPU utilization. By allowing training and generation to share the same GPUs, we eliminate idle time and reduce hardware requirements — achieving higher throughput even with fewer GPUs.

vLLM's sleep() feature is essential for large-scale colocation. It enables fine-grained control over memory usage, allowing training to fully reclaim GPU memory between generation steps — a key enabler for models like Qwen2.5-72B.

DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3 is essential for training large models. It allows extremely large networks to fit into memory by distributing model weights, gradients, and optimizer states across multiple GPUs. In our experience, enabling contiguous_gradients helped reduce memory fragmentation, while offloading the optimizer to the CPU freed up critical GPU memory — both of which were especially helpful in colocated setups.

Colocation is powerful but comes with trade-offs. It works best when GPU memory is carefully managed, often requiring manual tuning of memory usage parameters like vllm_gpu_memory_utilization. While it offers clear throughput benefits and reduces idle GPU time, colocation may not be ideal for models with tight memory budgets or when memory fragmentation is not well controlled. When done right, though, it unlocks significant efficiency gains.

TP/DP compatibility, Accelerate, and torchrun support make deployment seamless. Despite the complexity of the underlying architecture, the entire system can be launched and scaled with standard distributed tools.

Co-located training maintains model quality. Across multiple benchmarks (Math500, AIME24), co-located and plain setups produced comparable results, validating that performance isn’t sacrificed for efficiency.

This blog post explored how co-locating vLLM with GRPO training unlocks significant efficiency gains when training large language models — including models as large as Qwen2.5-72B.

Traditionally, TRL only supported vLLM in server mode, which required separate processes and GPUs for inference, leading to wasted compute and idle time. With the introduction of vLLM’s external launcher and the colocation PR in TRL PR #3394, we can now run training and inference within the same distributed process group, on the same GPUs, with full support for TP, DP, and Accelerate.

While challenges remain — such as version-specific vLLM bugs and edge cases such as with sleep() — the overall results show that co-located GRPO is a practical, scalable solution for training large models efficiently. We’re excited to continue refining this setup, integrating features like FSDP, and pushing the limits of large model training — making it faster, cheaper, and more accessible for everyone building the next generation of LLMs.

#10730. SmolVLA: Efficient Vision-Language-Action Model trained on Lerobot Community Data

Today, we introduce SmolVLA, a compact (450M), open-source Vision-Language-Action model for robotics that runs on consumer hardware.

Over the past few years, Transformers have driven remarkable progress in AI, from language models capable of human-like reasoning to multimodal systems that understand both images and text. However, in real-world robotics, advancements have been much slower. Robots still struggle to generalize across diverse objects, environments, and tasks. This limited progress stems from a lack of high-quality, diverse data and the absence of models that can reason and act like humans in the physical world.

In response to these challenges, the field has recently turned to vision-language-action (VLA) models, which aim to unify perception, language understanding, and action prediction within a single architecture. VLAs typically take as input raw visual observations and natural language instructions, and output corresponding robot actions. While promising, much of the recent progress in VLAs remains locked behind proprietary models trained on large-scale private datasets, often requiring costly hardware setups and extensive engineering resources. As a result, the broader robotics research community faces significant barriers in reproducing and building upon these models.

SmolVLA addresses this gap by offering an open-source, compact, and efficient VLA model that can be trained on consumer-grade hardware using only publicly available datasets. By releasing not only model weights but also using very affordable open-source hardware, SmolVLA aims to democratize access to vision-language-action models and accelerate research toward generalist robotic agents.

Figure 1: Comparison of SmolVLA across task variations. From left to right: (1) asynchronous pick-place cube counting, (2) synchronous pick-place cube counting, (3) pick-place cube counting under perturbations, and (4) generalization on pick-and-place of the lego block with real-world SO101.

SmolVLA-450M is our open-source, compact yet capable VLA model. It is:

Inspired by the training paradigms of Large Language Models (LLMs), SmolVLA goes through a pretraining phase on general manipulation data, followed by task-specific post-training. Architecturally, it combines Transformers with flow-matching decoders, and is optimized for speed and low-latency inference with the following design choices:

Despite using fewer than 30k training episodes—an order of magnitude less than other VLAs—SmolVLA matches or exceeds the performance of much larger models, both in simulation and the real world.

To make real-time robotics easier to use, we introduce an asynchronous inference stack. This technology separates how robots perform actions from how they understand what they see and hear. Because of this separation, robots can respond more quickly in fast-changing environments.

Figure 2. SmolVLA takes as input a sequence of RGB images from multiple cameras, the robot’s current sensorimotor state, and a natural language instruction. The VLM encodes these into contextual features, which condition the action expert to generate a continuous sequence of actions.

SmolVLA is designed to be easy to use and integrate—whether you're finetuning on your own data or plugging it into an existing robotics stack.

First, install the required dependencies:

Use smolvla_base, our pretrained 450M model, with the lerobot training framework:

​​If you'd like to build from the architecture (pretrained VLM + action expert) rather than a pretrained checkpoint:

You can also load SmolVLAPolicy directly:

SmolVLA is not only a lightweight yet capable model, but also a method for training and evaluating generalist robotics policies. In this section, we introduce the model architecture behind SmolVLA and the asynchronous inference setup used for evaluation, which has proven to be more adaptable and capable of faster recovery.

SmolVLA consists of two core components: a Vision-Language Model (VLM) that processes multimodal inputs and an action expert that outputs robot control commands. Below, we share the details of the main components of SmolVLA architecture and the Asynchronous Inference. More details can be found in our technical report.

We use SmolVLM2 as our VLM backbone. It’s optimized for multi-image inputs and consists of a SigLIP vision encoder and a SmolLM2 language decoder.

The decoder layers process concatenated image, language, and state tokens. The resulting features are then passed to the action expert.

SmolVLA’s action expert is a compact transformer (~100M parameters) that generates action chunks, i.e. sequences of future robot actions, conditioned on the VLM’s outputs. It is trained using a flow matching objective, which teaches the model to guide noisy samples back to the ground truth. In contrast, while discrete action representations (e.g., via tokenization) are powerful, they often require autoregressive decoding, which is slow and inefficient at inference time. While flow matching allows direct, non-autoregressive prediction of continuous actions, enabling real-time control with high precision.

More intuitively, during training, we add random noise to the robot’s real action sequences and ask the model to predict the “correction vector” that brings them back to the correct trajectory. This forms a smooth vector field over the action space, helping the model learn accurate and stable control policies.

We implement this using a transformer architecture with interleaved attention blocks (see the figure 2), and reduce its hidden size to 75% of the VLM’s, keeping the model lightweight for deployment.

While combining a vision-language model with an action prediction module is a common design pattern in recent VLA systems—such as Pi0, GR00T, Diffusion Policy — we identified several architectural choices that significantly enhance the robustness and performance. In SmolVLA, we apply three key techniques: reducing the number of visual tokens, skipping upper layers in the VLM, and interleaving cross- and self-attention layers in the action expert.

High-resolution images improve perception but can significantly slow down inference. To strike a balance, SmolVLA limits the number of visual tokens to 64 per frame during both training and inference. For example, a 512×512 image is compressed into just 64 tokens, instead of 1024, using PixelShuffle as an efficient shuffling technique. While the underlying Vision-Language Model (VLM) was originally pretrained using image tiling for broader coverage, SmolVLA uses only the global image at runtime to keep inference lightweight and fast.

Rather than always relying on the final layer of the VLM—which can be expensive and sometimes suboptimal—we use features from intermediate layers. Prior work has shown that early layers often provide better representations for downstream tasks. In SmolVLA, the action expert only attends to VLM features up to a configurable layer NN during training, set to half the total layers. This halves the compute cost of both the VLM and the action expert, significantly speeding up inference with minimal performance loss.

Inside the action expert, attention layers alternate between:

We found that this interleaved design is both lighter and more effective than using full attention blocks. Models that rely only on CA or only on SA tend to sacrifice either smoothness or grounding.

In SmolVLA, CA ensures that actions are well-conditioned on perception and instructions, while SA improves temporal smoothness—especially critical for real-world control, where jittery predictions can result in unsafe or unstable behavior.

Figure 3. Asynchronous inference. Illustration of the asynchronous inference stack. Note that the policy can be run on a remote server, possibly with GPUs.

Modern visuomotor policies output action chunks—sequences of actions to execute. There are two ways to manage them:

Our async stack decouples action execution from chunk prediction, resulting in higher adaptability, and the complete lack of execution lags at runtime. It relies on the following key mechanisms:

We are really excited about releasing asynchronous inference because it guarantees greater adaptability and improved performance without changing the model. In short, async inference keeps the robot responsive by overlapping execution and remote prediction.

While vision and language models thrive on web-scale datasets like LAION, ImageNet, and Common Crawl, robotics lacks a comparable resource. There’s no “Internet of robots.” Instead, data is fragmented across robot types, sensors, control schemes, and formats—forming disconnected "data islands". In our previous post, we explored how this fragmentation could be resolved through open, collaborative efforts. Just as ImageNet catalyzed breakthroughs in computer vision by providing a large, diverse benchmark, we believe that community-driven robotics datasets can play the same foundational role for generalist robot policies.

SmolVLA is our first step toward that vision: It is pretrained on a curated mix of publicly available, community-contributed datasets designed to reflect real-world variation. Rather than optimizing for dataset size alone, we focus on diversity: a range of behaviors, camera viewpoints, and embodiments that promote transfer and generalization.

All training data used in SmolVLA comes from LeRobot Community Datasets , robotics datasets shared on the Hugging Face Hub under the lerobot tag. Collected in diverse settings, from labs to living rooms, these datasets represent an open, decentralized effort to scale real-world robot data.

Figure 4. A glimpse of the community dataset. Special thanks to Ville Kuosmanen for creating the visualization. Unlike academic benchmarks, community datasets naturally capture messy, realistic interactions: varied lighting, suboptimal demonstrations, unconventional objects, and heterogeneous control schemes. This kind of diversity will be very useful for learning robust, general-purpose representations.

We used a customfiltering tool created by Alexandre Chapin and Ville Kuosmanen to select datasets based on frame count, visual quality, and task coverage. After a meticulous manual review (special thanks to Marina Barannikov), we curated a collection of 487 high-quality datasets focused on the SO100 robotic arm, standardized at 30 FPS. This yielded around 10 million frames—at least one order of magnitude smaller than other popular benchmark datasets, yet significantly more diverse.

A common issue across community datasets was noisy or missing task descriptions. Many episodes lacked annotations or included vague labels like “task desc” or “Move”, “Pick”. To improve quality and standardize the textual input across datasets, we used Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct to generate concise, action-oriented descriptions.

Given sample frames and the original label, the model was prompted to rewrite the instruction in under 30 characters, starting with an action verb (e.g., “Pick,” “Place,” “Open”).

Another challenge was inconsistent camera naming. Some datasets used clear names like top or wrist.right, while others used ambiguous labels like images.laptop, which varied in meaning. To fix this, we manually went through the datasets and mapped each camera view to a standardized scheme: OBS_IMAGE_1: Top-down view OBS_IMAGE_2: Wrist-mounted view OBS_IMAGE_3+: Additional viewpoints

We further isolate the contributions of community dataset pretraining and multitask finetuning. Without pretraining on the LeRobot community datasets, SmolVLA initially achieves 51.7% success on SO100. After pretraining on community-collected data, performance jumps to 78.3%, a +26.6% absolute improvement. Multitask finetuning further boosts performance, showing strong task transfer capabilities even in low-data regimes.

Table 1. Impact of Pretraining on Community Datasets and Multitask Finetuning.

We evaluate SmolVLA across simulation and real-world benchmarks to test its generalization, efficiency, and robustness. Despite being compact, It consistently outperforms or matches the performance of significantly larger models and policies pretrained on higher-scale robotics data.

Table 2. SmolVLA Performance on Simulation Benchmarks.

Table 3. SmolVLA vs Baselines on Real-World Tasks (SO100).

In real-world settings, SmolVLA is evaluated on two diverse suites: SO100 and SO101. These tasks include pick-place, stacking, and sorting, with both in-distribution and out-of-distribution object configurations. On SO101, SmolVLA also excels in generalization:

Table 4. Generalization of SmolVLA to New Embodiment (SO101) vs ACT..

Finally, we evaluate SmolVLA under synchronous and asynchronous inference modes. Async inference decouples action execution from model inference, allowing the policy to react while the robot is moving.

This results in more responsive and robust real-world performance, especially in dynamic environments with shifting objects or external disturbances.

Figure 5. Asynchronous vs. Synchronous Inference in Real-World Tasks. (a) Task success rates (%), (b) average completion time(s), and (c) number of tasks completed within a fixed time window.

SmolVLA is our contribution to building robotics foundation models that are open, efficient, and reproducible. Despite its small size, it matches or outperforms larger, proprietary models across a range of real-world and simulated tasks. By relying solely on community-contributed datasets and affordable hardware, SmolVLA lowers the barrier to entry for researchers, educators, and hobbyists alike. But this is just the beginning. SmolVLA is more than just a model — it's part of a growing open-source movement toward scalable, collaborative robotics.

Together, we can make real-world robotics more capable, more affordable, and more open. ✨

#10729. Holo1: New family of GUI automation VLMs powering GUI agent Surfer-H

Today, at H Company, we are releasing Holo1, a family of Action Vision Language Models (VLMs) and WebClick, a new multimodal localization benchmark on the Hugging Face Hub.

Surfer-H, a web-native agent that interacts with browsers like a human relies on the Holo1.

Holo1 is the first family of open-source Action VLMs designed specifically for deep web UI understanding and precise localization. The family includes Holo1-3B and Holo1-7B models, with the latter achieving 76.2% average accuracy on common UI localization benchmarks—the highest among small-size models. H Company has released these models with open-source on Hugging Face, along with the WebClick benchmark containing 1,639 human-like UI tasks.

Holo1 models are based on the Qwen2.5-VL architecture, and are fully compatible with transformers. Here we provide a simple usage example. You can load the model and the processor as follows.

Web automation represents one of AI's most practical applications for businesses, but until now, solutions have often sacrificed cost-efficiency for performance. By making our Holo1 Action Models available in Hugging Face, users can now implement web automation solutions that achieve 92.2% accuracy on real-world web tasks at only $0.13 per task.

Surfer-H relies on the Holo1 family of open-weights models. It is a modular architecture for complete web task automation, which performs reading, thinking, clicking, scrolling, typing, and validating. It is designed to be flexible and modular, composed of three independent components: a Policy model that plans and drives the agent's behavior, a Localizer model that understands visual UIs for precise interactions, and a Validator model that confirms whether tasks are completed successfully. Unlike other agents that rely on custom APIs or brittle wrappers, Surfer-H operates purely through the browser — just like a real user.

Together, these solutions represent a new frontier in web automation, achieving state-of-the-art localization performance and setting the Pareto frontier in cost-efficient web navigation on the WebVoyager benchmark:

By Michael Gamble, Partner & Ecosystem Lead, Arm

As a software engineer and music producer, I’m always exploring how technology can expand creative expression. That curiosity recently led me to build a personal sound generation app that runs directly on-device—powered by an Arm-based CPU and open-source generative AI models. It’s fast, private, and enables me to generate studio-ready sounds from a simple prompt, all within seconds.

This project brings together the best of several worlds:

When I’m deep in a music project using Ableton Live, I don’t want to interrupt my workflow to dig through libraries or browse sound packs. I wanted a tool that could meet me where I am—right in the flow.

Now, I can simply describe the sound I’m imagining (“analog bassline,” “cinematic riser,” “lofi snare”), and within seconds, the generated .wav file appears in my Ableton browser. From there, I can tweak it, loop it, or turn it into an instrument.

Every sound is unique. No one else will generate exactly what I do. That sense of personal ownership fuels my creativity.

This sound generator runs entirely on-device using Arm-based CPU technology—no GPU, no cloud inference, no latency. Thanks to Arm's efficiency and performance-per-watt, the app stays responsive even during multi-step diffusion runs.

#10727. How to Organize CSS with Cascade Layers in Large Web Projects

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

As a website grows, its stylesheet often becomes harder to maintain. A rule added to fix one component can unexpectedly affect another, and developers may find themselves adding increasingly specific selectors to override previous styles. Over time, these changes make CSS difficult to understand and update.

CSS cascade layers provide a way to organize styles into named groups and control their priority. Instead of relying entirely on selector specificity and the order of declarations, developers can establish a predictable structure for their stylesheets.

CSS determines which declarations apply by considering factors such as origin, importance, cascade layer priority, specificity, and source order. When several rules target the same element, understanding these factors helps explain why one style overrides another.

If all three rules apply to the same button under normal author styles, the ID selector wins because it has greater specificity.

This can become inconvenient when a project contains third-party styles, reusable components, and application-specific overrides. Developers may respond by adding more specific selectors, making future changes increasingly difficult.

Cascade layers offer another approach: establish a clear priority order before writing individual component rules.

A useful starting point is to divide styles according to their purpose. For example, a project might contain reset styles, third-party styles, reusable components, and page-specific adjustments.

You can establish these layers at the beginning of your stylesheet:

The declaration at the top establishes the order for normal declarations in these layers. For normal author styles, later layers have higher priority than earlier layers, regardless of selector specificity between those layers.

This means a simple selector in a higher-priority layer can override a more specific selector in a lower-priority layer.

For more background on building adaptable interfaces, developers can explore SitePoint's introduction to CSS container queries, which explains another way to structure maintainable component styles.

Not every project needs the same number of layers. A small website may require only a few, while a large application may benefit from a more detailed structure.

This is a suggested structure rather than a mandatory convention. The important part is defining the priority order intentionally and applying it consistently.

Cascade layers can help avoid selectors that become unnecessarily complicated.

For normal declarations, the second rule wins because overrides has higher layer priority, even though the first selector contains an ID and more class selectors.

This can make changes easier to review because developers do not need to keep increasing selector specificity to achieve the intended result.

However, layer order should not become an excuse to place every exception in a global override layer. Keep related styles close to their components and use overrides only when the exception is intentional.

Cascade layers have rules that developers need to understand before adopting them across an existing codebase.

For normal declarations, later layers have higher priority. For declarations marked !important, the layer priority is reversed. Important declarations in earlier layers take precedence over important declarations in later layers.

Unlayered normal author styles also take precedence over normal declarations inside author cascade layers. This matters when integrating a layered stylesheet with older CSS that remains outside the layer structure.

The MDN documentation on CSS cascade layers explains these priority rules and provides additional examples.

Before reorganizing a production stylesheet, test how existing third-party rules, inline styles, and important declarations interact with the new structure.

Rewriting an entire stylesheet at once can introduce regressions. A safer approach is to define the intended layer order, migrate one group of styles at a time, and compare the rendered interface after each change.

Start with styles that are easy to isolate, such as resets or a small set of reusable components. Check buttons, forms, navigation, and responsive layouts at several viewport sizes.

Browser developer tools can help identify which declaration is winning and whether it belongs to the expected layer. Visual regression tests are also useful when the application has many shared components.

For teams, documenting the layer order and agreeing on where new styles belong can prevent the stylesheet from becoming disorganized again.

CSS cascade layers provide developers with a practical way to manage style priority in growing applications. By separating resets, vendor styles, components, and utilities into a clear hierarchy, teams can reduce specificity conflicts and make stylesheets easier to maintain.

The best results come from a deliberate layer structure, consistent naming, and careful testing during migration. Cascade layers do not remove the need to understand CSS specificity, but they give developers another tool for controlling how styles interact.

#10726. KV Cache from scratch in nanoVLM

We have implemented KV Caching from scratch in our nanoVLM repository (a small codebase to train your own Vision Language Model with pure PyTorch). This gave us a 38% speedup in generation. In this blog post we cover KV Caching and all our experiences while implementing it. The lessons learnt are general and can be applied to all autoregressive language model generations. Implementing from scratch on a small codebase is a great learning experience, come along for the ride!

Autoregressive language models generate text by sampling one token at a time. During inference, the model processes a given input sequence, predicts the next token, appends it to the sequence, and repeats this process until some stopping criterion:

This step-by-step generation is inherently sequential:

This repetition also leads to computational redundancy. In this post, we explore KV Caching, an optimisation technique that mitigates this inefficiency.

Before diving into caching, let’s revisit how attention operates in transformer models. A Transformer language model consists of stacked layers, each composed of:

To understand where KV Caching helps, we focus on the self-attention mechanism, specifically within a single attention head.

Let’s walk through a simple PyTorch implementation to visualise the key computations.

For a sequence of T T T input embeddings represented as X∈RT×D X \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times D} X∈RT×D, self-attention is computed as:

Attention(X;Q,K,V)=softmax(QK⊤⋅Mdk)V \text{Attention}(X; Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left( \frac{QK^\top \cdot M}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right)V Attention(X;Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QK⊤⋅M​)V

Here’s a minimal PyTorch equivalent using a causal mask:

In autoregressive generation, the model generates one token at a time. With each step, it recomputes Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V for the entire sequence, even though the earlier tokens haven’t changed.

These checks show that for all but the newest token, K K K and V V V are identical to previously computed values.

Most of the attention computation is repeated needlessly. This gets more expensive as sequences grow.

To eliminate this inefficiency, we use KV Caching:

This changes generation from full-sequence re-computation to a lightweight, incremental update.

✅ In practice, this cache is a per-layer dictionary with keys "key" and "value", each of shape (batch_size, num_heads, seq_len_cached, head_dim).

This is the foundation of how modern LLMs can generate long outputs efficiently.

Now that we understand the theory behind KV Caching, let’s see how it’s implemented in practice inside our nanoVLM repository. This is an ideal testbed, as it's a super concise and self-contained codebase.

KV caching is enabled across three key components in our model:

In the LanguageModelGroupedAttention class, we modify the forward function to accept and update a cache of keys and values (block_kv_cache).

Previously, the model recomputed K K K and V V V at every generation step. Now we only compute Knew K_{\text{new}} Knew​, Vnew V_{\text{new}} Vnew​ for the current token, and append them to the cached values.

In the LanguageModel class, we introduce layer-wise cache tracking. The start_pos argument helps the model compute correct rotary positional encodings for newly generated tokens.

The biggest architectural change is in the generate() method of the VisionLanguageModel.

By separating these phases, we avoid redundant computation and dramatically speed up inference, especially for long prompts.

KV caching eliminates unnecessary computation during autoregressive generation, enabling faster and more efficient inference, especially in long sequences and real-time applications. This is a trade-off between speed and memory, and its drawbacks can be more complex code and restricting fancier inference schemes, like beam-search, etc. KV caching is a popular method for speeding up LLM inference, making it possible to run them on consumer hardware, and now you know how it works too!

#10725. ScreenSuite - The most comprehensive evaluation suite for GUI Agents!

Over the past few weeks, we’ve been working tirelessly on making GUI agents more open, accessible and easy to integrate. Along the way, we created the largest benchmarking suite for GUI agents performances 👉 let us introduce ScreenSuite.

We are very excited to share it with you today: ScreenSuite is the most comprehensive and easiest way to evaluate Vision Language Models (VLMs)across many agentic capabilities!

GUI Agents in action - courtesy of OSWorld

In short, an AI Agent is a robot that acts in the virtual world. (more thorough definition here)

In particular, a “GUI Agent” is an agent that lives in a GUI. Think “an agent that can do clicks and navigate on my desktop or my phone”, à la Claude Computer Use.

This means in essence that the AI model powering the agent will be given a task like “Fill the rest of this Excel column”, along with screen captures of the GUI. Using this information, it will then decide to take action on the system : click(x=130, y=540) to open a web browser, type(”Value for XYZ in 2025"), scroll(down=2) to read further… To see a GUI agent in action, you can try our Open Computer Agent, powered by Qwen2.5-VL-72B.

A good GUI agent will be able to navigate a computer just like we would, thus unlocking all computer tasks : scrolling through Google Maps, editing a file, buying an item online. This involves a variety of capabilities that can be hard to evaluate.

The literature, for instance Xu et al. (2025) or Qin et al. (2025), generally splits GUI agent abilities amongst several categories:

So our first contribution is to gather and unify a comprehensive suite of 13 benchmarks spanning the full range of these GUI agent capabilities.

If you look at the last category listed above, evaluating Multi-step agentic capabilities is especially challenging as it requires virtual machines to run the agent’s environment, be it Windows, Android, Ubuntu... To address this, we provide support both for E2B desktop remote sandboxes, and we created from scratch a new option to easily launch Ubuntu or Android virtual machines in Docker!

We’ve carefully designed our benchmark suite with modularity and consistency in mind, ensuring strong alignment across tasks and environments. When required, especially for online benchmarks, we leverage smolagents as framework layer to streamline agent execution and orchestration.

To support reproducibility and ease of use, we’ve built custom Dockerized containers that allow local deployment of full Ubuntu Desktop or Android environments.

Unlike many existing GUI benchmarks that rely on accessibility trees or other metadata alongside visual input, our stack is intentionally vision-only. While this can result in different scores on some established leaderboards, we deem that it creates a more realistic and challenging setup, one that better reflects how humans perceive and interact with graphical interfaces.

– All agentic frameworks (Android World, OSWorld, GAIAWeb, Mind2Web) use smolagents and rely solely on vision, without any accessibility tree or DOM added (in contrast with evaluation settings reported in other sources). – Mind2Web (Multimodal) originally used element-name-based multi-choice selection based on the accessibility tree and screenshots, but was later adapted to click precision within bounding boxes using vision only, which significantly increases task difficulty.

We’ve evaluated leading VLMs on the benchmark

Our scores are in general agreement with the scores reported in various sources! With the caveat that we evaluate on vision only, causing some differences, see implementation details above.

💡 Note that ScreenSuite does not intend to exactly reproduce benchmarks published in the industry: we evaluate models on GUI agentic capabilities based on vision. As a result, on benchmarks like Mind2Web where other benchmarks gave the agent a view of information rich context like DOM or accessibility tree, our evaluation setting is much harder, thus ScreenSuite does not match other sources.

The multistep benchmarks requires a bare-metal machine to run and deploy desktop/mobile* environment *emulators (see README.md)

Running consistent and meaningful evaluations easily allows the community to quickly iterate and make progress in this field, as we’ve seen with Eleuther LM evaluation harness, the Open LLM Leaderboard and the Chatbot Arena.

We hope to see much more capable open models in the coming month that can run a wide range of tasks reliably and even run locally!

#10724. Introducing Training Cluster as a Service - a new collaboration with NVIDIA

Today at GTC Paris, we are excited to announce Training Cluster as a Service in collaboration with NVIDIA, to make large GPU clusters more easily accessible for research organizations all over the world, so they can train the foundational models of tomorrow in every domain.

Many Gigawatt-size GPU supercluster projects are being built to train the next gen of AI models. This can make it seem that the compute gap between the “GPU poor” and the “GPU rich” is quickly widening. But the GPUs are out there, as hyperscalers, regional and AI-native cloud providers all quickly expand their capacity.

How do we then connect AI compute capacity with the researchers who need it? How do we enable universities, national research labs and companies all over the world to build their own models?

This is what Hugging Face and NVIDIA are tackling with Training Cluster as a Service - providing GPU cluster accessibility, with the flexibility to only pay for the duration of training runs.

To get started, any of the 250,000 organizations on Hugging Face can request the GPU cluster size they need, when they need it.

To get started, you can request a GPU cluster on behalf of your organization at hf.co/training-cluster

Training Cluster as a Service integrates key components from NVIDIA and Hugging Face into a complete solution:

Once your GPU cluster request is accepted, Hugging Face and NVIDIA will collaborate to source, price, provision and set up your GPU cluster per your size, region and duration requirements.

The Telethon Institute of Genomics and Medicine - TIGEM for short - is a research center dedicated to understanding the molecular mechanisms behind rare genetic diseases and developing novel treatments. Training new AI models is a new path to predict the effect of pathogenic variants and for drug repositioning.

AI offers new ways to research the causes of rare genetic diseases and to develop treatments, but our domain requires training new models. Training Cluster as a Service made it easy to procure the GPU capacity we needed, at the right time

We are tracking well on our objective to build open alternatives to the best closed-source models, such as Deepmind's AlphaProof. Computing resources is our bottleneck today - with Training Cluster as a Service we will be able to reach our goal!

-- Yann Fleureau, cofounder of Project Numina

Mirror Physics is a startup creating frontier AI systems for chemistry and materials science.

Together with the MACE team, we're working to push the limits of AI for chemistry. With Training Cluster as a Service, we're producing high-fidelity chemical models at unprecedented scale. This is going to be a significant step forward for the field.

-- Sam Walton Norwood, CEO and founder at Mirror

Training Cluster as a Service is a new collaboration between Hugging Face and NVIDIA to make AI compute more readily available to the global community of AI researchers.

Access to large-scale, high-performance compute is essential for building the next generation of AI models across every domain and language. Training Cluster as a Service will remove barriers for researchers and companies, unlocking the ability to train the most advanced models and push the boundaries of what’s possible in AI.

-- Clément Delangue, cofounder and CEO of Hugging Face

Integrating DGX Cloud Lepton with Hugging Face’s Training Cluster as a Service gives developers and researchers a seamless way to access high-performance NVIDIA GPUs across a broad network of cloud providers. This collaboration makes it easier for AI researchers and organizations to scale their AI training workloads while using familiar tools on Hugging Face.

#10723. Elder Scrolls 6 merch is being sold years before game is close to release

Bethesda is already selling official merchandise for The Elder Scrolls 6, despite the long-awaited RPG still being years away from release.

It’s been 15 years since Skyrim launched in 2011, and fans have been waiting for its sequel ever since Bethesda first announced the game back in 2018.

On November 3, the studio finally revealed that the next installment will be called The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel, although there was no gameplay footage or release date to accompany the announcement.

But while fans might have a lengthy wait before they can actually play the new game, they can already buy a T-shirt or hoodie to show their support.

Bethesda’s official merchandise store has started selling two items celebrating Sentinel, despite the game still being deep in development. The first is a black T-shirt priced at $34.99, while the second is a matching hoodie for $64.99.

Both feature branding for the upcoming RPG and share a similar description that reads: “Your next journey through Tamriel will be in The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel. Show off your excitement with the official tee!”

However, there’s still no indication of when players will actually get their hands on the game itself. Bloomberg journalist Jason Schreier suggested that Sentinel is still more than two years away from launching.

That would put a potential release in late 2028 at the earliest, although Bethesda hasn’t announced a launch window. The developer also made it clear that fans shouldn’t expect another major reveal anytime soon.

“Development continues, and while it’ll be some time before we’re ready to share more, it feels great to finally reveal the name and location with you,” Bethesda said in its November 3 announcement.

Elder Scrolls VI reportedly still more than 2 years away despite Bethesda finally revealing its name

Elder Scrolls 6 name and setting reportedly confirmed after fans already worked it out

Elder Scrolls 6 fans convinced they’ve uncovered the name after Xbox CEO clue

So, while there’s no telling when Sentinel will finally arrive, fans can at least get their hands on some official merch to tide themselves over.

NVIDIA Isaac GR00T (Generalist Robot 00 Technology) is a research and development platform for building robot foundation models and data pipelines, designed to accelerate the creation of intelligent, adaptable robots.

Today, we announced the availability of Isaac GR00T N1.5, the first major update to Isaac GR00T N1, the world’s first open foundation model for generalized humanoid robot reasoning and skills. This cross-embodiment model processes multimodal inputs, including language and images, to perform manipulation tasks across diverse environments. It is adaptable through post-training for specific embodiments, tasks, and environments.

In this blog, we’ll demonstrate how to post-train (fine-tune) GR00T N1.5 using teleoperation data from a single SO-101 robot arm.

#10721. GTA 6 boss defends delays with nod to Cyberpunk 2077’s launch

Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick referenced Cyberpunk 2077’s launch as a reason why GTA 6 has needed to be delayed.

With the clock quickly ticking towards November 19, Grand Theft Auto fans are closer than ever to getting their hands on GTA 6. The day seemed like it would never come, especially after two initial delays.

Rockstar Games stated that those delays were necessary to release the game in the state that fans “deserve” and “expect” from them. The second delay did come as a surprise to Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick, who was eventually won over by Rockstar’s reasoning.

The delays came up during his chat with the Wall Street Journal, with Zelnick making a nod towards Cyberpunk 2077’s fated launch.

“There are a lot of companies who have a great mission statement, a stated strategy, and a culture, but then when push comes to shove, you know, they do something that’s at odds with that,” he said.

Zelnick noted that some developers choose to be “slavishly devoted to a schedule” and ship games regardless. That led to his Cyberpunk and CD Projekt Red nod.

“I’m not going to throw any competitors under the bus, but if you know anything about the video game business, in the past few years, there was a very high-profile release that fell into this category, and they shipped, and they had to pull the title after shipping because it didn’t work.”

As Zelnick notes, Cyberpunk 2077 was removed from stores, including Sony’s PlayStation marketplace, with refunds being offered to players as well.
